Algorithm Theoretical Basis Document

Joint Multi-Atmosphere Bin Retrieval for Along-Slit Keystone/Smile Correction

A state-space, nearest-bin (or interpolated) joint estimator that recovers a per-along-slit-position CO₂ field from a keystone- and smile-distorted GeoCarb-like focal plane, in place of native's one-atmosphere-per-detector-row assumption.

Instrument: GeoCarb FPA2 (simulated) Scene: noise-free, realistic along-slit CO₂ Example used throughout: rows 890–935, G=15

1Purpose and Scope

Native GeoCarb-style Level 2 retrieval fits one atmospheric state per detector row. Because the real focal plane exhibits keystone (wavelength-dependent spatial magnification) and smile (position-dependent spectral curvature), a single row's own 1024 columns do not sample one true along-slit position — they sample a range of positions that widens with keystone amplitude. Fitting one atmosphere to that spliced mixture systematically dilutes any real, spatially localized signal: a simulated CO₂ point source at high keystone recovers only 44% of its true peak-to-background enhancement under native retrieval, versus 99% for an idealized undistorted instrument.

This document describes a joint, multi-atmosphere alternative: partition the along-slit coordinate into G discrete bins, assign every real detector pixel to its nearest bin by its own exact along-slit position, and solve for all G atmospheric states simultaneously against every real pixel in a neighborhood — never interpolating or blending measured radiances. Two ways of turning those G bin values into predicted pixel radiances are both covered: a coarse scheme (nearest-bin assignment) and a hi-res scheme (the same G values interpolated onto native detector-row resolution before radiative transfer). §4 walks through the shared pipeline both schemes use and shows exactly where they diverge.

2Terminology

Two layers of terms are used throughout: physical/geometric quantities that exist independent of any retrieval design choice, and modeling quantities that are choices made in building this specific estimator.

Physical / geometric layer

TermDefinition
sceneThe true atmospheric state along the slit — state(η) → AtmosphericProfile (along_slit_scene.atmosphere_at). Radiance is derived from the scene, not the scene itself: radiance(η) = RT(state(η)), computed by running that state through ForwardModel.
η (eta)Normalized along-slit position, η ∈ [−1, 1]. xkm = η × SLIT_HALF_KM is the same quantity in physical distance; the mapping is a fixed bijection, so state can be indexed by either.
pixelOne detector element at row i, column j. Has its own exact true (η(i,j), ν(i,j)) from the real ground-test dispersion polynomials, and one measured/predicted radiance A[i,j].
footprintThe along-slit domain that physically contributes to a given pixel's — or a given retrieval's — measured value. Widened by keystone, by the spatial PSF, and, for a regularized joint retrieval, by the prior's own correlation length (§6).
rowOne horizontal line of 1024 pixels sharing detector row index i. Not a single along-slit position — its footprint is a range of η, which is the mechanism behind the dilution bias this method addresses.

Retrieval / modeling layer

TermDefinition
binA segment of the η-axis, with one representative center, to which a single atmospheric state is assigned in the joint state vector. G is the number of bins — equivalently, the number of free parameters the retrieval solves for.
coarse attributionEvery pixel is assigned its nearest bin's own spectrum, unmodified — a step function of η. No interpolation of radiance, ever.
anchor / G_effHi-res attribution's own fine grid: one control point per real detector row in the padded neighborhood. G_eff is fixed by the row window and padding alone, independent of G — it is a ceiling on how finely hi-res can resolve the state, not a free-parameter count.
hi-res attributionThe G retrieval values are linearly interpolated (in state space) onto the G_eff anchors before radiative transfer — a piecewise-linear function of η instead of coarse's step function.
neighborhoodThe contiguous range of rows over which one joint solve runs.
atmosphere / stateThe physical quantity assigned to each bin or anchor. In general a full AtmosphericProfile; in the example used throughout this document, a scalar co2_scale multiplying a bin-specific local prior atmosphere.

3Physical Basis: the Known Distortion Operator

Unlike a generic ill-posed deconvolution problem, the distortion here is known exactly. Detector-plane position maps to (wavelength, along-slit position) via ground-test-calibrated polynomials, xy_to_wavelength_slit(fpa, col, row) → (λ, s). Three effects compose to determine a pixel's true sample position:

EffectCharacterConsequence for one row's footprint
keystoneSpatial magnification varies with wavelengthA row's own columns sweep a range of η that grows with keystone amplitude — measured by rows_crossed(fpa, row), an endpoint-to-endpoint difference in row-equivalent units.
smileSpectral position curves quadratically with ηCan produce real within-row structure even where the endpoint difference reads near zero.
spatial PSFAlong-slit (row-to-row) blur, ~1.5 px FWHM, applied via gaussian_blur_rowsGenuinely mixes true radiance across neighboring rows — the one place cross-row mixing in the forward model is physically correct rather than an artifact.

Because the distortion operator is known rather than estimated, this is a classical (if non-separable) forward-modeling problem: every pixel's exact (η, ν) is computable in closed form, and the estimation task is choosing what atmospheric state to assign at each along-slit position given that known mapping.

4The Pipeline, Step by Step

The single governing rule behind every step below: a pixel's predicted radiance is computed by running radiative transfer once, on a real atmospheric state, then convolving at that pixel's own exact wavenumber. Two continuous spectra are never blended together to produce a third. This is not a stylistic preference — bilinearly interpolating already-rendered pixel radiances is the mechanism responsible for the largest bias found anywhere in this line of investigation (an approximately −62 ppm CO₂ bias from a rectify-then-retrieve pipeline, present even on a spatially uniform scene). Every step here is illustrated on the same concrete example: FPA2, rows 890–935, G=15 bins placed by pixel density (§5), with bin 6 (η=0.7475, 416.71 ppm) sitting under the true hot spot and bin 0 (η=0.7014, 413.00 ppm) representing background.

1Define an atmospheric state at each bin center

For bin g at position ηg, build the local atmosphere via als.atmosphere_at(x_km_g) — the same function that generates the real scene's per-position truth — with the free co2_scale parameter (one entry of the retrieval's state vector) scaling CO₂. Every other quantity (H₂O, CH₄, CO, surface pressure) is fixed to that position's own local truth.

2Run radiative transfer to get a continuous spectrum per bin

ForwardModel(atm, absco, instrument, geometry, solver, solar).run(albedo=...) maps each bin's atmosphere to a hi-res spectrum S(ν) on a dense wavenumber grid — a function of wavelength only, not yet tied to any detector pixel. The CO₂ contrast between bins is a small fraction of the total radiance (here, about 0.6% peak-to-peak), so it is only visible as a difference, not in the raw spectra themselves.

3Determine each pixel's own exact position

xy_to_wavelength_slit(fpa, col, row) gives every detector pixel its own exact (η, ν) from the real dispersion polynomials — a purely geometric step, independent of any atmospheric state. Plotting a few rows in the (η, ν) plane shows what keystone and smile actually do: each row sweeps the full spectral range at a nearly fixed η, tracing a curve rather than a straight vertical line.

4Attribute a spectrum to each pixel

This is where the two schemes diverge. Both operate per pixel, using that pixel's own exact η from Step 3 — never a single value shared across a whole row.

Coarse: each pixel is assigned its nearest bin's own spectrum from Step 2, unmodified (nearest_bin_scene). Row 910 alone, because its own columns span a real range of η, draws its 1024 pixels' spectra from 4 different bins.

Hi-res: the same G=15 retrieval values are first linearly interpolated (in co2_scale, i.e. in state space) onto G_eff=54 anchors — one per real detector row in the padded window — each anchor getting its own freshly-computed spectrum from Step 2's own recipe. Pixels are then assigned to their nearest anchor. Row 910 now draws from 10 distinct anchors instead of 4 distinct bins.

5Convolve at the pixel's own exact wavenumber

Whichever spectrum Step 4 attributed to a pixel is convolved against the ILS (instrument spectral response function) centered exactly at that pixel's own ν from Step 3 — a normalized, weighted average over a narrow spectral window, not a lookup of the nearest hi-res sample.

6Assemble the unblurred image

Steps 3–5 repeat for every column of every row in a padded window, producing a full-resolution radiance array — one row per real detector row, no cross-row mixing yet. The dominant visible structure at this stage is spectral (column-direction absorption lines), since the CO₂ contrast between rows is small by comparison.

7Apply the spatial PSF blur

gaussian_blur_rows convolves the assembled array along the row axis with a normalized ~1.5 px FWHM Gaussian — the one place real cross-row mixing happens anywhere in this pipeline. To make the smoothing visible against the much larger spectral structure from Step 6, the same kernel is shown here applied schematically to the bin-assigned CO₂ value itself (rather than to radiance at one wavelength), which makes the effect easy to see: a discontinuous step function in, a smooth curve out.

8Compare against the real measurement

The result of Steps 1–7 is a predicted detector image. Subtracting it from the real measured image, pixel by pixel, gives the residual the Gauss–Newton solve minimizes (§6). §8 shows what that residual looks like for both attribution schemes, and what it reveals about where each one is accurate.

5Bin Definition and Placement

Choosing where the G bin centers sit is a separate question from how attribution works (§4). Two rules are compared, both placing G=15 centers across the same rows 890–935 window:

SchemeRuleRationale
uniformEvenly spaced across the neighborhood's η rangeBaseline; bin density constant regardless of local distortion.
pixel‑densityEvenly-spaced quantiles of the actual per-pixel η distribution in the neighborhoodWherever keystone is large, more rows' footprints overlap a given η interval, so real pixel density is genuinely higher there — both because native's dilution problem is worse there and because more independent pixels support a finer bin there.

Peak-enhancement capture (retrieved rise between the hot spot and a background row, as a fraction of the true rise) was 81.7% for uniform bins and 90.9% for pixel-density bins at G=15 — a real difference, though this particular window under-exercises the scheme's actual design goal (concentrating resolution specifically where keystone is large and starving it where keystone is small), since it is uniformly high-keystone throughout.

6Joint Estimation

State vector and observation model

The state is x = [x1…xG], one co2_scale per bin — the only free parameter anywhere in the state; every nuisance gas is fixed to its own local truth (§4, Step 1). The observation vector y is every real pixel's measured radiance in the neighborhood, raveled; the forward operator F(x) is Steps 1–7 of §4, run either the coarse or hi-res way.

Regularized Gauss–Newton update

Rodgers update
Δx = (KTSy−1K + Sa−1)−1 (KTSy−1·resid − Sa−1·(x−xa))
Prior precision — first-difference Tikhonov smoothness
Sa−1 = γ·(LTL) + σabs−2I

where L is the first-difference operator penalizing differences between adjacent bins' values, and σabs is a loose absolute floor keeping the system well-posed against the Laplacian's own null space (a uniform shift of every bin together). The solve is joint — one linear system per iteration for all G bins — not G independent per-bin fits smoothed together afterward.

γ is an assumed correlation length

The regularization strength encodes a claim about how correlated the true CO₂ field is at the scale of one bin spacing. If the true field is smoother than that assumption, information genuinely propagates between neighboring bins — legitimate, the same logic as any optimal-estimation prior. If the true field is sharper, the same term actively biases the result by pulling estimates toward neighbors that don't really resemble them — a version of the dilution problem this method exists to fix, now sourced from the prior instead of from row-splicing.

GERTRetrieval is deliberately not reused. Its StateVector.apply() maps onto exactly one AtmosphericProfile, its constructor takes exactly one ForwardModel/StateVector pair, and its Gauss–Newton step is not factored out separately from that single-atmosphere plumbing — subclassing or monkey-patching to fake a multi-atmosphere state would be more fragile than the small standalone solver built on the pieces that generalize cleanly (StateVector.gas_scaling()/.apply() and ForwardModel, both reused unmodified).

8Error Characterization

For an audience accustomed to OCO-2's Rodgers-form error budget — smoothing error, forward-model parameter error, retrieval noise — the useful framing is: native retrieval's dilution bias is an extreme, uncharacterized smoothing error. A single-atmosphere-per-row fit implicitly assumes an averaging kernel of the identity when the real footprint says otherwise. This method's whole contribution is to make that averaging kernel wider than the identity on purpose, using real information about where along the slit resolution can and can't be recovered.

8.1 — Quantization: coarse step function vs. hi-res interpolation

Representing a continuously-varying field with G discrete states, attributed by nearest-neighbor lookup, introduces an error proportional to local curvature — largest at a peak, negligible on smooth background. Solving the identical G=15 problem both ways, on the identical scene, isolates exactly this effect: nothing else about the state, the pixels, or the truth changes between the two solves.

GschemeRMS biasmax |bias|capturemean bin χ²
15coarse0.257 ppm1.081 ppm90.9%1.87×10−8
15hi-res0.133 ppm0.563 ppm89.8%5.24×10−9
30coarse0.129 ppm0.554 ppm97.6%4.03×10−9
30hi-res0.060 ppm0.232 ppm97.0%5.54×10−9

Two trends hold across both G tested: doubling G roughly halves bias for either scheme, and hi-res holds a steady ~2× bias advantage over coarse at both — not an artifact of one particular G.

Goodness-of-fit does not track this improvement as cleanly — hi-res's mean bin χ² was lower than coarse's at G=15 but very slightly higher at G=30. Retrieval bias and residual quality measure different things: χ² is about explaining the observed pixels given whatever state was found, while bias is about whether that state matches truth. χ² alone would be a misleading proxy for retrieval accuracy here.

8.2 — The resolution floor is not just bin width

A bin's actual footprint — the along-slit domain its one retrieved value represents an average over — has two contributors, only one of which shrinks with G: bin/anchor assignment width, which the modeler controls, and the spatial PSF's own ~1.5 px blur, already irreversibly baked into every pixel's measured value before attribution ever happens (§4, Step 7). Once G (or G_eff) pushes assignment width below the PSF's own footprint, further refinement stops adding real resolution — it chops an already-smoothed signal into more, increasingly redundant labels. The rigorous tool for characterizing this, not yet built, is the generalized averaging kernel A = (KTSy−1K + Sa−1)−1KTSy−1K, exactly analogous to the vertical averaging kernels OCO-2's own L2 full-physical retrieval reports, applied here in the along-slit spatial dimension.

8.3 — Point-sample vs. footprint-integrated forward model

Every pixel, in both the synthetic truth generator and this forward model, is evaluated at an exact point sample of the scene — state(η) — which is then run through RT exactly once. Neither side explicitly integrates over a pixel's own finite footprint width. This matters because RT is nonlinear in state (absorption-line saturation), so footprint-averaging is only physically correct done after RT, in radiance space; averaging the scene first and running RT once on that average is a different, generally wrong quantity, the same mechanism by which the spatial PSF's own physical blending of bright/dark true radiances differs from blending their states first. A Taylor expansion of the correct quantity shows the point-sample error is second order: negligible where the radiance response is locally linear in η, systematically overstating peak amplitude where it has real curvature. Because both sides of every residual use the same point-sample approximation, this does not distort the comparisons in this document — but it means even an idealized undistorted instrument's own reported ~99% capture may be somewhat optimistic relative to what any physically real detector, with finite pixels performing genuine footprint integration in radiance space, could ever measure. Not yet quantified.

8.4 — Idealizations in the example used throughout

  • Nuisance gases are fixed to each bin's or anchor's own local true value rather than jointly retrieved — isolating the CO₂ bin-splicing question from a separate, larger free-nuisance-state engineering problem.
  • Sy−1 is a simple uniform relative weighting, not the instrument's real photon-noise model — acceptable on a still-noise-free scene where the limiting factor is model mismatch, not noise-weighted averaging.
  • No measurement noise has been added anywhere in this document.
